Triggers on: explore the codebase, understand the architecture, what functions exist, show me the structure, who calls this function, what does X call, trace the call chain, find callers of, show dependencies, impact analysis, dead code, unused functions, high fan-out, refactor candidates, code quality audit, graph query syntax, Cypher query examples, edge types, how to use search_graph.

BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

60	-- Seed the default source. 'default' is federated=true for backward compat
61	-- (pre-v0.17 brains behave exactly as before — every page appears in search).
62	-- Pre-existing sync.repo_path / sync.last_commit are copied in by the v16
63	-- migration, not here; fresh installs have no local_path until `sources add`
64	-- or the first `sync`.
65	INSERT INTO sources (id, name, config)
66	  VALUES ('default', 'default', '{"federated": true}'::jsonb)

70	-- so POST /webhooks/github's source-by-repo lookup hits an index. Only rows
71	-- with a configured webhook actually take up index entries. Both Postgres and
72	-- PGLite support partial expression indexes. Migration v87 installs the same
73	-- index on legacy brains (idempotent IF NOT EXISTS).
74	CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS sources_github_repo_idx
75	  ON sources ((config->>'github_repo'))

82	-- Slugs are unique per source, NOT globally. The default source is
83	-- seeded in the sources block above so the DEFAULT 'default' FK is
84	-- always valid at INSERT time.
85	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pages (
86	  id            SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
87	  source_id     TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'default'
88	                REFERENCES sources(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
89	  slug          TEXT    NOT NULL,

91	  -- v0.19.0: distinguishes markdown vs code pages at the DB level.

93	  page_kind     TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'markdown'

95	  title         TEXT    NOT NULL,
96	  compiled_truth TEXT   NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
97	  timeline      TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
98	  frontmatter   JSONB   NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
99	  content_hash  TEXT,
100	  -- v0.29: deterministic 0..1 score (tag emotion + take density + Garry-as-holder ratio).
101	  -- Populated by the `recompute_emotional_weight` cycle phase. Default 0.0 so freshly
102	  -- imported pages don't pollute salience ranking before the cycle has run.
103	  emotional_weight REAL NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.0,
104	  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
105	  updated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
106	  -- v0.26.5: soft-delete + recovery window. `delete_page` sets deleted_at = now()
107	  -- instead of issuing DELETE. The autopilot purge phase hard-deletes pages
108	  -- where deleted_at < now() - 72h. Search and `get_page` filter
109	  -- `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` by default; `include_deleted: true` opts in.
110	  deleted_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
111	  -- v0.29.1: salience-and-recency, additive opt-in. All NULL by default;
112	  -- only consulted when a caller passes `salience='on'` / `recency='on'` or
113	  -- the new `since`/`until` filter. effective_date_source is a sentinel for
114	  -- the doctor's effective_date_health check (values: 'event_date' | 'date'
115	  -- | 'published' | 'filename' | 'fallback'). salience_touched_at is bumped
116	  -- by recompute_emotional_weight when emotional_weight changes so the
117	  -- salience window picks up newly-salient old pages.
118	  effective_date        TIMESTAMPTZ,

121	  salience_touched_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
122	  -- v0.37.0 (migration v79): real stale-page signal for `gbrain lsd`. Bumped
123	  -- by op-layer write-back inside `search`/`query`/`get_page` op handlers
124	  -- (NOT inside engine methods — internal callers must not pollute the
125	  -- signal). NULL = never retrieved (LSD prioritizes these first).
126	  last_retrieved_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,

139	  -- haiku_model, title_wrapper_version, embedding_model) — document-side

146	  -- counter bumped by bump_page_generation_trg on INSERT (initial value =
147	  -- MAX(generation) + 1 so the bookmark fires for any cache row stored
148	  -- before this page existed — codex #4) and on UPDATE when any column in

157	-- bumps generation per D6 / codex #4. INSERT: pages get
158	-- COALESCE(MAX(generation), 0) + 1 so the bookmark gate fires for any
159	-- cache row stored before the new page existed. UPDATE: bumps only when

-- (pre-v0.17 brains behave exactly as before — every page appears in search).
-- Pre-existing sync.repo_path / sync.last_commit are copied in by the v16

  VALUES ('default', 'default', '{"federated": true}'::jsonb)
  ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;

-- so POST /webhooks/github's source-by-repo lookup hits an index. Only rows
-- with a configured webhook actually take up index entries. Both Postgres and

-- index on legacy brains (idempotent IF NOT EXISTS).

  ON sources ((config->>'github_repo'))
  WHERE config ? 'github_repo';

-- seeded in the sources block above so the DEFAULT 'default' FK is
-- always valid at INSERT time.

  title         TEXT    NOT NULL,
  compiled_truth TEXT   NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  timeline      TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  frontmatter   JSONB   NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  content_hash  TEXT,
  -- v0.29: deterministic 0..1 score (tag emotion + take density + Garry-as-holder ratio).
  -- Populated by the `recompute_emotional_weight` cycle phase. Default 0.0 so freshly

  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

1	---
2	title: Modeling Memory in a Knowledge-Base Agent
3	status: draft
4	audience: wakil design
5	---
6	
7	# Modeling Memory in a Knowledge-Base Agent
8	
9	A knowledge base that only accumulates degrades. Every note added raises the
10	odds that the next search returns near-duplicates, that a stale fact outranks
11	the correction that replaced it, and that the one useful record is buried under
12	forty redundant ones. Human memory faces the same three problems — things fade,
13	things resurface, and similar things interfere — and it solves them with
14	mechanisms that map cleanly onto design choices for an agent like wakil.
15	
16	This paper works through those mechanisms one at a time, pairs each with its
17	agentic analog, and closes with a concrete model for wakil that stays inside the
18	project's constraints: Markdown as the source of truth, SQLite as the
19	operational index, a candidate-to-active memory lifecycle, and human review for
20	anything that changes durable content.
21	
22	The central claim is one distinction, borrowed from the memory literature and
23	worth stating up front: **how retrievable a memory is** and **whether it is
24	stored at all** are different variables. Human forgetting is mostly the first,
25	not the second. Copy that split and you get graceful forgetting and surprise
26	recall from the same machinery, without ever destroying data.
27	
28	## Fading
29	
30	Four distinct things get called "forgetting," and they call for different
31	responses.
32	
33	**Decay from disuse.** Traces weaken over time when not accessed. The
34	forgetting curve is roughly exponential — a steep initial drop, then a long
35	tail. Pure time-based decay is contested as a sole mechanism; much of what looks
36	like decay is interference wearing a disguise. The agentic analog is a
37	recency-and-frequency weight on each record: a score that falls with time and
38	rises with use. Cheap to compute, and it needs no background process if it's
39	derived from a last-accessed timestamp on read.
40	
41	**Interference.** Often the larger driver. New information competes with old,
42	old competes with new, and similar traces blur together. This is the "which
43	parking spot today" failure — two hundred near-identical memories overwrite each
44	other into mush. In a knowledge base this is the dominant failure mode, not a
45	footnote, so it gets its own section below.
46	
47	**Retrieval failure.** A large fraction of forgetting is not lost storage. The
48	trace is intact; the cue that reaches it is missing or too weak. The information
49	is there and the index is broken. This is the single most useful idea to carry
50	into the design: down-weight the index, keep the data.
51	
52	**Consolidation failure.** Some memories were never durable. Low attention, no
53	salience, no rehearsal — they didn't fade, they never solidified. The analog is
54	a record ingested but never cited, never linked, never confirmed. It should be
55	easy to let those lapse.
56	
57	Set against these is one more, which is a feature rather than a fault.
58	
59	**Adaptive forgetting.** The brain prunes on purpose. Forgetting discards
60	outdated, low-value information so the signal isn't drowned by noise. It's a
61	compression strategy. An agent that treats forgetting only as loss will keep
62	everything and search will rot; an agent that treats controlled forgetting as
63	maintenance stays useful as it grows.
64	
65	## Resurfacing
66	
67	The other half of the question: why do forgotten things come back, sometimes
68	suddenly. The answers all follow from retrieval failure being reversible.
69	
70	**Cue encounter.** The dominant reason. A context, phrase, or associated concept
71	happens to match the missing retrieval path, and the trace lights up. The memory
72	was there the whole time; you found the door. The analog is direct: a query
73	whose terms overlap a dormant record's associations should be able to surface
74	it, even when that record sits below the normal ranking threshold.
75	
76	**Spreading activation.** Thinking about a concept partially activates its
77	neighbors. Enough accumulated partial activation crosses a threshold and the
78	memory arrives — which is why "thinking around it" works and why the answer
79	turns up minutes after you stopped trying. The analog is retrieval that isn't a
80	flat lookup: activating one record lends weight to linked records, so a
81	related-but-not-matching note can still come up.
82	
83	**Release from interference.** Stepping away lets competing traces settle so the
84	target is no longer crowded out. The analog is that a record suppressed by a
85	dense cluster of similar records becomes reachable once the cluster is thinned
86	or once a more specific cue distinguishes it.
87	
88	**Reconsolidation.** Each recall reopens a memory for editing. A retrieved
89	memory becomes briefly more accessible and can be rewritten, strengthened, or
90	corrupted before it settles again. This is the subtle one, and it's where a
91	naive design goes wrong, so it gets its own section too.
92	
93	## Reconsolidation, in detail
94	
95	The obvious implementation — strengthen a memory every time it appears in a
96	result — is wrong, and not only for the concurrency reasons covered below.
97	Semantic retrieval returns many candidates, most of them noise for any given
98	query. If mere candidacy strengthens a record, the records that win are the ones
99	that keep matching, not the ones that prove useful. Retrieval popularity is not
100	value. Left unchecked it's a rich-get-richer runaway.
101	
102	The fix starts by splitting one variable into three.
103	
104	- **Activation** — a fast-decaying "recently touched" signal. Bump it freely on
105	  retrieval; it's cheap, noisy, and self-erasing. This is the real analog of the
106	  temporary post-recall accessibility, and nothing durable should hang off it.
107	- **Strength** — the slow, valuable score. It updates only on a confirmation
108	  signal, with diminishing returns, and decays on its own.
109	- **Content** — the text of the memory. Rewritten only on a meaningful event,
110	  never on every touch.
111	
112	With that split, the interesting property of biological reconsolidation
113	survives: recall isn't monotonic strengthening. It opens a window in which the
114	memory can go up, down, or sideways depending on what happens in the window. The
115	driver is prediction error, not the access itself. A memory that keeps being
116	confirmed generates less and less surprise, so its updates shrink toward nothing
117	on their own — the ceiling is emergent, not imposed. A memory that's contradicted
118	gets rewritten or demoted. New associated information triggers a merge or a
119	re-summary.
120	
121	As a scalar, a saturating update captures the same bounded behavior:
122	
123	```text
124	strength += alpha * (ceiling - strength) * signal   # confirmation, saturating
125	strength -= beta  * strength                          # decay over time
126	```
127	
128	The increment shrinks as strength rises, decay pulls the other way, and the
129	record settles at an equilibrium that reflects its genuine confirmed-use rate.
130	Bounded, not runaway. The equilibrium level is the useful information.
131	
132	That leaves the load-bearing question: what is the confirmation signal? Mere
133	candidacy is the wrong answer. The right ones are downstream evidence that the
134	memory did work — it was cited in an answer, the answer was accepted, or it was
135	confirmed or contradicted by newer authoritative content. Without one of those,
136	prediction error is a metaphor with nothing to measure.
137	
138	## Interference, in detail
139	
140	Everything above is per-record: strength, decay, and reconsolidation each look
141	at one memory in isolation. Interference is relational — a property of pairs and
142	clusters. No per-record mechanism produces it. It has to be added as something
143	that reasons about neighbors, and it shows up in three places that map onto the
144	three human forms.
145	
146	**Write time — resolve it structurally.** When a new memory arrives, compare it
147	against what's already stored. The near-neighbors fall into four buckets, and
148	the right action differs for each:
149	
150	- **Duplicate** — merge, raise a support count, don't store a second copy.
151	- **Refinement** — same topic with more detail; re-summarize into one richer
152	  record.
153	- **Contradiction** — stale versus fresh; this is not a merge. Supersede by
154	  recency and version the old one out.
155	- **Coincidental similarity** — close in embedding space, genuinely different
156	  facts; keep both, and link them so retrieval can tell them apart.
157	
158	The naive rule `similar -> merge` collapses all four into the first two and
159	quietly corrupts the base. The real operation is a classifier plus an action,
160	not a similarity threshold.
161	
162	**Read time — interference as crowding.** Top-k scoring judges each record
163	against the query independently, so a cluster of near-duplicates sweeps the top
164	slots and starves diverse-but-relevant results. That is interference: redundant
165	traces drowning the signal. The standard fix is diversity-aware selection, where
166	each pick penalizes later picks that resemble it:
167	
168	```text
169	score(item) = lambda * sim(query, item)
170	            - (1 - lambda) * max sim(item, already_selected)
171	```
172	
173	The framing is lateral inhibition — selecting a record suppresses its neighbors
174	for that query. It lets you carry a cluster's worth (one representative plus its
175	support count) without letting the cluster crowd the results.
176	
177	**Confirmation time — retrieval-induced forgetting.** In people, recalling one
178	item suppresses its competitors; retrieving A makes B harder to reach later. The
179	analog reuses the confirmation signal from reconsolidation and gives it a second
180	job. When one record wins — gets cited, drives an accepted answer — raise it and
181	lower its uncited near-duplicates:
182	
183	```text
184	strength[w] += alpha * (ceiling - strength[w]) * signal        # winner up
185	strength[d] -= gamma * sim(w, d) * signal   for d != w         # crowd down
186	```
187	
188	Over many queries a redundant cluster collapses toward its best representative,
189	with no one deciding to delete the rest. They decay below threshold from
190	repeated non-selection. That is how the biology thins redundancy, and it's
191	cheap.
192	
193	Two failure modes to design against, both from treating similar records as
194	interchangeable. First, fifty copies of a fact are not fifty votes; track
195	support count and independent-source count separately, and weight by provenance,
196	not raw multiplicity. Second, over-merging destroys real distinctions — "4B on
197	Tuesdays" and "4C on Thursdays" are close in embedding space and are different
198	facts. Here copying human behavior, which famously smears similar episodes
199	together, is the bug. Bias merges conservative, require more than embedding
200	proximity before collapsing two records, and keep merges reversible.
201	
202	## Where this meets wakil's principles
203	
204	One tension has to be named directly. The clean engineering answer to
205	reconsolidation and interference is an asynchronous background worker that
206	rewrites and merges memories on its own — single-writer per record, debounced,
207	calling a model to re-summarize. That design is correct in the abstract and
208	wrong for wakil. The project's stated biases rule out hidden background
209	behavior and automatic rewriting of user knowledge without review. Silent
210	reconsolidation is exactly the thing wakil exists not to do.
211	
212	So the proposal below keeps the mechanisms and drops the autonomy. Scalars that
213	are cheap, deterministic, and reversible run on their own. Anything that changes
214	durable Markdown is a proposal surfaced for review, expressed as a diff, gated
215	on confirmation or the existing candidate-to-active promotion flow. Cost: the
216	base won't self-maintain while you sleep, and some cleanup waits on a human.
217	Why it's right anyway: in a personal knowledge base the whole value is trust in
218	the content, and a wrong silent merge costs more than a slow one.
219	
220	## Proposal: a concrete model for wakil
221	
222	Memories already live in SQLite as `candidate` records for review and promotion.
223	Extend that record, add a lifecycle, and attach the mechanisms above to events
224	wakil already has — ingest, index, search, and query.
225	
226	**State on each memory record.** Keep the Markdown notes as the source of truth
227	and hold the dynamics in SQLite, where they belong as operational state:
228	
229	- `strength` — the durable score, a float, default low.
230	- `activation` — fast-decaying recency signal; derived, not stored long.
231	- `last_accessed`, `access_count`, `cited_count` — the raw inputs to both above.
232	- `support_count`, `source_count` — multiplicity versus independent provenance,
233	  kept apart on purpose.
234	- `state` — one of `candidate`, `active`, `dormant`, `archived`.
235	- `supersedes` / `superseded_by` — contradiction lineage, so nothing is
236	  destroyed by a correction.
237	
238	**Lifecycle.** `candidate` on ingest, as today. Promotion to `active` on human
239	confirmation or first citation in an accepted answer. Demotion to `dormant` when
240	strength decays past a floor — still stored, still searchable, just below the
241	surfacing threshold, which is the retrieval-failure analog. `archived` only by
242	explicit action, and even then recoverable through git history. No state
243	transition deletes a Markdown file.
244	
245	**Decay, computed lazily.** No background job. Derive the current score from
246	`last_accessed` and `access_count` at read time, or fold it in during the
247	explicit `wakil index` pass. Deterministic, cheap, and it respects the ban on
248	hidden behavior because it only runs when the user runs a command.
249	
250	**Interference at ingest.** wakil's ingest already finds related notes and shows
251	a preview before writing. Extend that step with the four-way classifier —
252	duplicate, refinement, contradiction, coincidence — and put its verdict in the
253	preview. The user confirms a merge, a supersede, or "keep both, link them." The
254	model proposes; the human decides; the result is a reviewable diff. This is the
255	same shape as the current confirm-before-write flow, with a sharper suggestion
256	inside it.
257	
258	**Diversity at search.** Apply the lateral-inhibition penalty when assembling
259	results, so a cluster of near-duplicates contributes one representative plus its
260	support count instead of ten rows. This changes ranking only; it touches no
261	stored content and needs no review.
262	
263	**Confirmation from query.** `query` already records runs. Record which memories
264	were actually cited in an accepted answer, and treat that as the confirmation
265	signal: raise the cited record's strength on the saturating curve, and apply the
266	small retrieval-induced decrement to its uncited near-duplicates. Both are scalar
267	updates to SQLite, reversible and invisible to the Markdown.
268	
269	**Reconsolidation as a reviewable proposal.** When a citation or a contradiction
270	suggests a memory's content should change, wakil does not rewrite it. It emits a
271	reconsolidation candidate — a proposed edit or merge — into the same review
272	queue ingest uses, as a git diff. Approved, it lands as a normal reviewable
273	commit; declined, nothing changes. The labile window becomes a pull request,
274	not a silent edit.
275	
276	The one distinction to hold onto is the same one from the top: separate how
277	retrievable a memory is from whether it's stored. Retrievability is dynamic,
278	scalar, automatic, and reversible. Storage and content are Markdown, changed
279	only through review. That single split gives wakil human-like forgetting and
280	resurfacing while keeping every promise in `CLAUDE.md`.
281	
282	## Summary map
283	
284	| Human mechanism | Agentic analog | wakil mechanism |
285	| --- | --- | --- |
286	| Decay from disuse | Recency/frequency weight | `strength` from `last_accessed`, computed on read/index |
287	| Interference | Similarity competition | Four-way classifier at ingest; diversity penalty at search |
288	| Retrieval failure | Low index weight, data intact | `dormant` state — below threshold, still searchable |
289	| Consolidation failure | Never-cited record lapses | `candidate` that's never promoted |
290	| Adaptive forgetting | Controlled pruning | Demotion and archival, recoverable via git |
291	| Cue encounter | Term/association overlap | Query surfaces dormant records on match |
292	| Spreading activation | Linked-record boost | Activation lent across wikilinks |
293	| Reconsolidation | Prediction-error update | Scalar strength update; content changes as reviewed diffs |
294	| Retrieval-induced forgetting | Winner up, crowd down | Citation raises one, decrements near-duplicates |
295

job. When one record wins — gets cited, drives an accepted answer — raise it and
lower its uncited near-duplicates:

```text
strength[w] += alpha * (ceiling - strength[w]) * signal        # winner up
strength[d] -= gamma * sim(w, d) * signal   for d != w         # crowd down
```

Over many queries a redundant cluster collapses toward its best representative,
with no one deciding to delete the rest. They decay below threshold from
repeated non-selection. That is how the biology thins redundancy, and it's
cheap.

Two failure modes to design against, both from treating similar records as
interchangeable. First, fifty copies of a fact are not fifty votes; track
support count and independent-source count separately, and weight by provenance,
not raw multiplicity. Second, over-merging destroys real distinctions — "4B on
Tuesdays" and "4C on Thursdays" are close in embedding space and are different
facts. Here copying human behavior, which famously smears similar episodes
together, is the bug. Bias merges conservative, require more than embedding
proximity before collapsing two records, and keep merges reversible.

## Where this meets wakil's principles

One tension has to be named directly. The clean engineering answer to
reconsolidation and interference is an asynchronous background worker that
rewrites and merges memories on its own — single-writer per record, debounced,
calling a model to re-summarize. That design is correct in the abstract and
wrong for wakil. The project's stated biases rule out hidden background
behavior and automatic rewriting of user knowledge without review. Silent
reconsolidation is exactly the thing wakil exists not to do.

So the proposal below keeps the mechanisms and drops the autonomy. Scalars that
are cheap, deterministic, and reversible run on their own. Anything that changes
durable Markdown is a proposal surfaced for review, expressed as a diff, gated
on confirmation or the existing candidate-to-active promotion flow. Cost: the
base won't self-maintain while you sleep, and some cleanup waits on a human.
Why it's right anyway: in a personal knowledge base the whole value is trust in
the content, and a wrong silent merge costs more than a slow one.

## Proposal: a concrete model for wakil

Memories already live in SQLite as `candidate` records for review and promotion.
Extend that record, add a lifecycle, and attach the mechanisms above to events
wakil already has — ingest, index, search, and query.

**State on each memory record.** Keep the Markdown notes as the source of truth
and hold the dynamics in SQLite, where they belong as operational state:

- `strength` — the durable score, a float, default low.
- `activation` — fast-decaying recency signal; derived, not stored long.
- `last_accessed`, `access_count`, `cited_count` — the raw inputs to both above.
- `support_count`, `source_count` — multiplicity versus independent provenance,
  kept apart on purpose.
- `state` — one of `candidate`, `active`, `dormant`, `archived`.
- `supersedes` / `superseded_by` — contradiction lineage, so nothing is
  destroyed by a correction.

**Lifecycle.** `candidate` on ingest, as today. Promotion to `active` on human
confirmation or first citation in an accepted answer. Demotion to `dormant` when
strength decays past a floor — still stored, still searchable, just below the
surfacing threshold, which is the retrieval-failure analog. `archived` only by
explicit action, and even then recoverable through git history. No state
transition deletes a Markdown file.

**Decay, computed lazily.** No background job. Derive the current score from
`last_accessed` and `access_count` at read time, or fold it in during the
explicit `wakil index` pass. Deterministic, cheap, and it respects the ban on
hidden behavior because it only runs when the user runs a command.

**Interference at ingest.** wakil's ingest already finds related notes and shows
a preview before writing. Extend that step with the four-way classifier —
duplicate, refinement, contradiction, coincidence — and put its verdict in the
preview. The user confirms a merge, a supersede, or "keep both, link them." The
model proposes; the human decides; the result is a reviewable diff. This is the
same shape as the current confirm-before-write flow, with a sharper suggestion
inside it.

**Diversity at search.** Apply the lateral-inhibition penalty when assembling
results, so a cluster of near-duplicates contributes one representative plus its
support count instead of ten rows. This changes ranking only; it touches no
stored content and needs no review.

**Confirmation from query.** `query` already records runs. Record which memories
were actually cited in an accepted answer, and treat that as the confirmation
signal: raise the cited record's strength on the saturating curve, and apply the
small retrieval-induced decrement to its uncited near-duplicates. Both are scalar
updates to SQLite, reversible and invisible to the Markdown.

**Reconsolidation as a reviewable proposal.** When a citation or a contradiction
suggests a memory's content should change, wakil does not rewrite it. It emits a
reconsolidation candidate — a proposed edit or merge — into the same review
queue ingest uses, as a git diff. Approved, it lands as a normal reviewable
commit; declined, nothing changes. The labile window becomes a pull request,
not a silent edit.

The one distinction to hold onto is the same one from the top: separate how
retrievable a memory is from whether it's stored. Retrievability is dynamic,
scalar, automatic, and reversible. Storage and content are Markdown, changed
only through review. That single split gives wakil human-like forgetting and
resurfacing while keeping every promise in `CLAUDE.md`.

## Summary map

| Human mechanism | Agentic analog | wakil mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decay from disuse | Recency/frequency weight | `strength` from `last_accessed`, computed on read/index |
| Interference | Similarity competition | Four-way classifier at ingest; diversity penalty at search |
| Retrieval failure | Low index weight, data intact | `dormant` state — below threshold, still searchable |
| Consolidation failure | Never-cited record lapses | `candidate` that's never promoted |
| Adaptive forgetting | Controlled pruning | Demotion and archival, recoverable via git |
| Cue encounter | Term/association overlap | Query surfaces dormant records on match |
| Spreading activation | Linked-record boost | Activation lent across wikilinks |
| Reconsolidation | Prediction-error update | Scalar strength update; content changes as reviewed diffs |
| Retrieval-induced forgetting | Winner up, crowd down | Citation raises one, decrements near-duplicates |

"""SQLite schema for wakil's operational store.

The data model is single-user today but keeps user_id columns so the same
schema can serve multiple users later. Markdown stays the source of truth;
these tables index, cache, and record operational history.
"""

from datetime import UTC, datetime

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, String, Text, UniqueConstraint
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


def utcnow() -> datetime:
    return datetime.now(UTC)


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    display_name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(default=utcnow)


class Workspace(Base):
    __tablename__ = "workspaces"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    root_path: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(Text)

1	"""Markdown file discovery and metadata extraction."""
2	
3	import hashlib
4	import re
5	from dataclasses import dataclass, field
6	from pathlib import Path
7	
8	import frontmatter
9	
10	# Directories never indexed as knowledge content.
11	SKIPPED_DIRS = {".git", ".wakil", ".obsidian", "node_modules", ".venv"}
12	
13	_H1_RE = re.compile(r"^#\s+(.+?)\s*$", re.MULTILINE)
14	
15	
16	@dataclass
17	class MarkdownFile:
18	    """Metadata extracted from one Markdown file in the knowledge base."""
19	
20	    path: Path  # relative to the workspace root
21	    title: str
22	    content_hash: str
23	    metadata: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
24	
25	
26	def discover_markdown_files(root: Path) -> list[Path]:
27	    """Return workspace-relative paths of all indexable Markdown files."""
28	    results: list[Path] = []
29	    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*.md")):
30	        relative = path.relative_to(root)
31	        if any(part in SKIPPED_DIRS or part.startswith(".") for part in relative.parts[:-1]):
32	            continue
33	        results.append(relative)
34	    return results
35	
36	
37	def read_markdown_file(root: Path, relative_path: Path) -> MarkdownFile:
38	    """Parse one Markdown file into indexable metadata.
39	
40	    Malformed frontmatter must not break indexing: fall back to treating the
41	    whole file as plain content.
42	    """
43	    full_path = root / relative_path
44	    raw = full_path.read_bytes()
45	    content_hash = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
46	    text = raw.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
47	
48	    try:
49	        post = frontmatter.loads(text)
50	        metadata = dict(post.metadata)
51	        body = post.content
52	    except Exception:
53	        metadata = {}
54	        body = text
55	
56	    title = _extract_title(metadata, body, relative_path)
57	    return MarkdownFile(
58	        path=relative_path, title=title, content_hash=content_hash, metadata=metadata
59	    )
60	
61	
62	def _extract_title(metadata: dict, body: str, relative_path: Path) -> str:
63	    for key in ("title", "name"):
64	        value = metadata.get(key)
65	        if isinstance(value, str) and value.strip():
66	            return value.strip()
67	    match = _H1_RE.search(body)
68	    if match:
69	        return match.group(1)
70	    return relative_path.stem
71

1	# wakil: Local Knowledge-Work Agent Plan
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	`wakil` is a local-first AI agent for working with a personal Markdown knowledge base.
6	
7	The goal is not to build a broad agent platform, a coding assistant, or a complex multi-runtime system. The goal is to build a simple, pragmatic, powerful local assistant that helps a single user ingest, search, connect, revise, and reason over a Markdown knowledge base.
8	
9	The target knowledge base is GBrain / Obsidian style: Markdown files, links, concepts, notes, project material, meeting transcripts, web clippings, and other personal knowledge artifacts.
10	
11	The guiding product thesis is:
12	
13	> Build a local, git-native knowledge-work agent that helps a single user discover useful connections, maintain a Markdown knowledge base, and turn raw inputs into durable, searchable memory.
14	
15	The guiding engineering principle is:
16	
17	> Keep the implementation simple unless added complexity has a clear and self-evident impact on the target use case.
18	
19	Do not over-engineer this project.
20	
21	Any additional abstraction, service, datastore, runtime, interface, or agent behavior must directly support the local knowledge-work use case.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Name
26	
27	The project is named:
28	
29	```text id="rgwvfs"
30	wakil
31	```
32	
33	`wakil` should be treated as a local assistant, representative, or advocate for the user’s knowledge base.
34	
35	---
36	
37	## Target Use Case
38	
39	The target user is a single person working locally with a personal Markdown knowledge base.
40	
41	The core use case is not coding.
42	
43	The core use case is knowledge work:
44	
45	1. Ingest meeting transcripts.
46	2. Ingest meeting recordings after transcription.
47	3. Ingest Twitter/X links.
48	4. Ingest web articles.
49	5. Ingest pasted notes, outlines, and rough ideas.
50	6. Search existing Markdown knowledge.
51	7. Discover relationships between notes, people, topics, decisions, and ideas.
52	8. Generate useful summaries, briefs, maps, and follow-up notes.
53	9. Propose edits to the Markdown knowledge base.
54	10. Use git history to understand how the knowledge base has evolved.
55	11. Use pull requests or branches for larger ingests and modifications.
56	12. Run deeper reflection or “dream” passes that create unexpected but useful connections.
57	13. Use preexisting Claude or Hermes skills.
58	
59	The platform should be built for one local user first, while keeping the data model ready for multiple users later.
60	
61	---
62	
63	## Explicit Non-Goals
64	
65	Do not build these in the initial version:
66	
67	```text id="2qv19p"
68	coding agent workflows
69	remote Docker execution
70	multi-user hosted web app
71	Slack gateway
72	email gateway
73	browser automation framework
74	multi-agent swarms
75	desktop app
76	mobile app
77	complex distributed job system
78	fine-tuning
79	marketplace
80	large plugin architecture
81	enterprise permissions
82	cloud-first architecture
83	```
84	
85	The first version should be a rich local CLI for a single user working with a Markdown knowledge base.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## Product Shape
90	
91	`wakil` should feel like a thoughtful command-line companion for a personal knowledge base.
92	
93	The CLI should be the primary interface.
94	
95	It should be rich and pleasant to use:
96	
97	* clear commands;
98	* helpful previews;
99	* colorized diffs;
100	* progress indicators;
101	* structured tables;
102	* readable Markdown output;
103	* interactive confirmations;
104	* branch / PR guidance;
105	* summaries that are easy to paste back into notes;
106	* citations to source files, sections, commits, or ingested artifacts.
107	
108	The first version should not require a server, browser UI, or remote runtime.
109	
110	However, the design should not prevent additional interfaces later.
111	
112	---
113	
114	## Core Concepts
115	
116	### Knowledge Base
117	
118	The knowledge base is a local Markdown directory.
119	
120	It may follow GBrain, Obsidian, or similar conventions.
121	
122	A knowledge base contains:
123	
124	```text id="gw0j64"
125	Markdown notes
126	internal links
127	tags
128	frontmatter
129	attachments
130	transcripts
131	ingested articles
132	source metadata
133	concept notes
134	project notes
135	people notes
136	meeting notes
137	daily notes
138	decision records
139	```
140	
141	`wakil` should treat the Markdown knowledge base as the source of truth.
142	
143	SQLite is an index, cache, memory store, and operational database. It should not replace the Markdown files.
144	
145	### Workspace
146	
147	A workspace is a local knowledge-base checkout.
148	
149	A workspace contains:
150	
151	```text id="2rc70v"
152	Workspace
153	  id
154	  name
155	  root_path
156	  git_remote
157	  qmd_config
158	  memory_database
159	  ingest_directory
160	  generated_directory
161	  conventions
162	```
163	
164	The workspace boundary matters. `wakil` should not casually operate outside the configured knowledge base directory.
165	
166	### Source
167	
168	A source is raw material brought into the knowledge base.
169	
170	Examples:
171	
172	```text id="nhhyb0"
173	meeting transcript
174	meeting recording
175	Twitter/X link
176	web article
177	PDF
178	pasted note
179	audio transcript
180	email export
181	GitHub issue
182	existing Markdown file
183	```
184	
185	Each source should have metadata:
186	
187	```text id="ityl60"
188	source type
189	origin URL or file path
190	retrieved_at
191	author if known
192	published_at if known
193	title
194	content hash
195	ingest status
196	related notes
197	```
198	
199	### Note
200	
201	A note is a Markdown file in the knowledge base.
202	
203	Notes are durable user-facing knowledge artifacts.
204	
205	`wakil` may create or edit notes, but changes should be git-visible and reviewable.
206	
207	### Memory
208	
209	Memory should be uniform and easy to reason about.
210	
211	A memory is a structured claim, observation, relationship, summary, or working context derived from sources and notes.
212	
213	All memory should share one core model, even if different memory records have different lifecycle states.
214	
215	A memory record may represent:
216	
217	```text id="k5j1ed"
218	a fact
219	a summary
220	a relationship
221	a question
222	a hypothesis
223	a user preference
224	a project convention
225	a note-level embedding target
226	a source-level summary
227	a recurring theme
228	a decision
229	an unresolved thread
230	```
231	
232	### Skill
233	
234	A skill is a reusable Markdown procedure that teaches `wakil` how to perform a recurring knowledge-work task.
235	
236	Examples:
237	
238	```text id="3fnnwq"
239	ingest a meeting transcript
240	summarize an article
241	extract people and organizations
242	create an evergreen concept note
243	find connections between two topics
244	prepare a weekly synthesis
245	run a dream pass
246	```
247	
248	Skills should remain simple Markdown files, and use the same structure, conventions and format as Claude skills so that existing skills can be "dropped in" and used.
249	
250	---
251	
252	## Anti-Overengineering Rule
253	
254	Every added component must pass this test:
255	
256	```text id="5q4s95"
257	Does this clearly improve local Markdown knowledge work for one user?
258	```
259	
260	If the answer is not obviously yes, do not build it yet.
261	
262	Examples:
263	
264	| Idea                   |    Build Now? | Reason                                            |
265	| ---------------------- | ------------: | ------------------------------------------------- |
266	| Rich CLI               |           Yes | Primary product surface                           |
267	| SQLite                 |           Yes | Simple local persistence and indexing             |
268	| QMD integration        |           Yes | First-class search mechanism                      |
269	| Git integration        |           Yes | Knowledge base is file-native and history matters |
270	| Docker runtime         |            No | Not needed for local knowledge work               |
271	| Hosted web app         |            No | Not needed for first version                      |
272	| Multi-user auth        |            No | Data model only should be ready                   |
273	| Neo4J                  |   Maybe later | Useful only if graph exploration proves valuable  |
274	| Background daemon      | Not initially | Use explicit CLI commands first                   |
275	| Multi-agent delegation |            No | Adds complexity without immediate need            |
276	
277	
278	Maintain a `TODO.md` with items to work on in the future.
279	
280	---
281	
282	## Architecture
283	
284	The initial architecture should be deliberately simple.
285	
286	```text id="nca2l1"
287	CLI
288	  commands, prompts, rich output
289	
290	Application Services
291	  ingest
292	  search
293	  query
294	  memory
295	  dream
296	  notes
297	  git
298	  qmd
299	
300	Local Storage
301	  SQLite
302	  Markdown files
303	  Git repository
304	  QMD index/config
305	
306	Model Layer
307	  provider abstraction
308	  prompt builders
309	  structured outputs
310	
311	Integrations
312	  QMD
313	  Git
314	  GitHub CLI
315	  web article fetcher
316	  transcript/audio tooling
317	```
318	
319	There should be no runtime abstraction beyond what is necessary to keep local execution clean.
320	
321	Do not build Docker, remote execution, or hosted services in the first version.
322	
323	---
324	
325	## Suggested Python Stack
326	
327	Use modern Python and boring local infrastructure.
328	
329	```text id="olf5zd"
330	Python 3.12+
331	uv
332	Pydantic v2
333	Typer
334	Rich / Textual-friendly output patterns
335	SQLite
336	SQLAlchemy
337	Alembic
338	httpx
339	BeautifulSoup / readability-lxml for article extraction
340	python-frontmatter
341	markdown-it-py
342	PyYAML
343	GitPython or subprocess git wrapper
344	pytest
345	ruff
346	ty
347	```
348	
349	Model access should be provider-abstracted but minimal:
350	
351	```text id="p1muyf"
352	OpenAI-compatible endpoint
353	Anthropic
354	Gemini or other provider later only if needed
355	local model endpoint later if useful
356	```
357	
358	Search:
359	
360	```text id="lch4np"
361	QMD as first-class search
362	SQLite FTS5 for internal records
363	optional embeddings later
364	optional Neo4J deep dive later
365	```
366	
367	---
368	
369	## Proposed Repository Structure
370	
371	```text id="9rx558"

696	
697	## Memory Model
698	
699	Memory is central to `wakil`.
700	
701	The model should be uniform, but memory should have lifecycle behavior.
702	
703	### Memory Lifecycle
704	
705	Use a simple lifecycle:
706	
707	```text id="fqhcpc"
708	working → candidate → durable
709	                  ↘ rejected
710	durable → archived
711	```
712	
713	Definitions:
714	
715	| State       | Meaning                                                    |
716	| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
717	| `working`   | Temporary context from a session, query, or ingest         |
718	| `candidate` | Potentially useful memory proposed by the system           |
719	| `durable`   | Approved or promoted memory that should affect future work |
720	| `rejected`  | Memory proposal that should not be used                    |
721	| `archived`  | Old memory retained for history but downranked             |
722	
723	This allows memory to “fade” without inventing too much machinery.
724	
725	### Fading
726	
727	Rather than delete memory, `wakil` should reduce the retrieval priority of memory that is old, weak, unreferenced, or never promoted.
728	
729	A simple ranking formula can combine:
730	
731	```text id="ptz8zd"
732	state
733	importance
734	freshness
735	confidence
736	recency
737	number of references
738	whether linked to a durable note
739	whether confirmed by user action
740	```
741	
742	Working memories should naturally fade unless they are promoted.
743	
744	Candidate memories should remain visible for review but not dominate search.
745	
746	Durable memories should be favored.
747	
748	Archived memories should be searchable but not prominent.
749	
750	Memories should be vector indexed for similarity search, and their applicability weighted by their relevance, recency, confidence, and number of references.
751	
752	### Promotion
753	
754	Memory can migrate to long-term durable memory through:
755	
756	```text id="1uystx"
757	explicit user approval
758	being incorporated into a Markdown note
759	being referenced repeatedly
760	being produced by a trusted skill
761	being confirmed during a dream pass
762	```
763	
764	Do not make this too magical at first.
765	
766	In the initial version, explicit promotion is enough.
767	
768	---
769	
770	## Dream Function
771	
772	A “dream” function is a deeper synthesis pass inspired by GBrain.
773	
774	The purpose of dreaming is not to hallucinate. The purpose is to search the knowledge base in a less literal way and propose useful connections, questions, and synthesis notes.
775	
776	A dream pass may:
777	
778	```text id="uzlsog"
779	review recent working and candidate memories
780	search QMD for related notes
781	look for recurring themes
782	find weak or surprising relationships
783	cluster related ideas
784	identify unresolved questions
785	propose new concept notes
786	propose links between existing notes
787	suggest memories to promote or archive
788	produce a human-readable dream report
789	```
790	
791	The dream output should be reviewable.
792	
793	A dream should not automatically rewrite the knowledge base unless explicitly approved.
794	
795	Initial dream command:
796	
797	```bash id="jwpq32"
798	wakil dream
799	```
800	
801	Useful variants:
802	
803	```bash id="08y0u2"
804	wakil dream --recent
805	wakil dream --topic "insurance claims automation"
806	wakil dream --since "2 weeks ago"
807	wakil dream --source transcript.md
808	wakil dream --write-report
809	wakil dream --propose-links
810	```
811	
812	Dream should produce:
813	
814	```text id="qtqtgj"
815	summary
816	interesting connections
817	possible contradictions
818	open questions
819	suggested durable memories
820	suggested note links
821	suggested notes to create
822	source citations
823	```
824	
825	Dream is a good place to explore more sophisticated memory behavior later.
826	
827	---
828	
829	## Search and Relationship Discovery
830	
831	Search and discovery are core.
832	
833	`wakil` should use QMD as a first-class search mechanism.
834	
835	### Search Sources
836	
837	Use multiple simple search paths:
838	
839	```text id="pmtlaf"
840	QMD search over Markdown knowledge base
841	SQLite FTS5 over sources, memories, query runs, and indexed note metadata
842	git history search
843	optional relationship table traversal
844	```
845	
846	Initial search should be hybrid but pragmatic.
847	
848	Do not build an elaborate RAG framework.
849	
850	### QMD Integration
851	
852	QMD should be treated as the primary knowledge-base search engine.
853	
854	`wakil` should be able to:
855	
856	```text id="p6y7e8"
857	detect QMD config
858	run QMD queries
859	map QMD results back to note paths
860	show QMD results in CLI output
861	use QMD results as context for LLM queries
862	combine QMD results with SQLite memory records
863	```
864	
865	The QMD integration should be encapsulated so that the rest of the app does not depend on shell command details.
866	
867	### Relationship Discovery
868	
869	Relationship discovery should begin simply.
870	
871	For an ingest or query, `wakil` can extract candidate relationships like:
872	
873	```text id="xl0cne"
874	Source A mentions Concept B
875	Note A relates to Note B
876	Memory A supports Memory B
877	Memory A raises Question B
878	Topic A appears in the same context as Topic B
879	```
880	
881	Relationships should be treated as candidate signals unless promoted or repeatedly supported.
882	
883	Do not require Neo4J initially.
884	
885	---
886	
887	## Optional Neo4J Deep Dive
888	
889	Neo4J may become valuable if relationship exploration becomes central.
890	
891	Potential benefits:
892	
893	```text id="4ka4h4"
894	visual graph exploration
895	multi-hop relationship queries
896	concept clustering
897	people / project / topic networks
898	stronger dream passes
899	relationship-heavy browsing
900	```
901	
902	Reasons not to add it initially:
903	
904	```text id="f9qmar"
905	adds operational complexity
906	requires graph modeling decisions too early
907	duplicates what SQLite can handle at small scale
908	may distract from the Markdown-first workflow
909	```
910	
911	Recommended approach:
912	
913	1. Start with SQLite relationship tables.
914	2. Build useful relationship extraction and review.
915	3. Evaluate whether SQLite becomes limiting.
916	4. Add optional Neo4J export or sync only if graph workflows prove valuable.
917	
918	Initial stance:
919	
920	```text id="h7zmyh"
921	SQLite first. Neo4J later as an optional enhancement, not a core dependency.
922	```
923

926	## Git-Native Workflow
927	
928	`wakil` should be git-native.
929	
930	The Markdown knowledge base should be treated like a real repository.

933

999

1035	## Ingest Workflow
1036	
1037	Ingest is one of the most important workflows.
1038	
1039	Supported initial ingest types:
1040	
1041	```text id="d177u9"
1042	local Markdown file
1043	whisper zip archive with transcript in JSON format

1048	```

1052	### Ingest Steps
1053	
1054	A simple ingest flow:
1055	
1056	```text id="02qv2h"
1057	receive source
1058	capture source metadata
1059	extract text
1060	store raw text or source reference with appropriate metadata
1061	summarize source
1062	search QMD for related notes
1063	extract candidate memories
1064	extract candidate relationships
1065	propose note changes

1071	
1072	Each ingest should produce:
1073	
1074	```text id="z5zlf0"

1076	summary
1077	key points
1078	related existing notes
1079	candidate new notes
1080	candidate memories
1081	candidate relationships
1082	proposed Markdown changes
1083	citations back to source
1084	git diff if files changed
1085	```
1086	
1087	The user should be able to accept, reject, or modify proposed changes.

1519	memory fading in retrieval ranking
1520	memory citations
1521	```
1522	
1523	Success criterion:
1524	
1525	```text id="pppjmf"
1526	wakil can propose, review, promote, and downrank memories.
1527	```
1528	
1529	### Phase 6: Dream
1530	
1531	Goal: build a useful synthesis mode.
1532	
1533	Build:
1534	
1535	```text id="7vaplm"
1536	recent memory review
1537	topic-based dream
1538	relationship suggestions
1539	open question extraction
1540	concept note proposals
1541	dream report output
1542	optional write-report mode
1543	```
1544	
1545	Success criterion:
1546	
1547	```text id="gxjt58"
1548	wakil can produce a non-obvious but grounded synthesis report from existing notes and memories.
1549	```
1550	
1551	### Phase 7: Optional Graph Deep Dive
1552	
1553	Goal: decide whether Neo4J is worth adding.
1554	
1555	Build only if needed:
1556	
1557	```text id="m5myab"
1558	export SQLite relationships to graph format
1559	prototype Neo4J import
1560	test multi-hop queries
1561	compare value versus SQLite traversal
1562	```
1563	
1564	Success criterion:
1565	
1566	```text id="5p2tfa"
1567	Neo4J proves clearly useful for relationship discovery beyond what SQLite and QMD provide.
1568	```
1569	
1570	---
1571	
1572	## Near-Term Implementation Tasks
1573	
1574	A good initial Codex task list:
1575	
1576	1. Create the `wakil` Python project with `uv`.
1577	2. Add `Typer`, `Rich`, `Pydantic`, SQLite support, and test tooling.
1578	3. Implement `wakil init`.
1579	4. Create local workspace config.
1580	5. Create SQLite schema for workspace, source, note, memory, relationship, ingest run, and query run.
1581	6. Implement Markdown file discovery and metadata indexing.
1582	7. Detect whether the workspace is a git repository.
1583	8. Detect whether QMD is available and configured.
1584	9. Implement a QMD search wrapper.
1585	10. Implement `wakil status`.
1586	11. Implement `wakil search`.
1587	12. Implement a minimal model client abstraction.
1588	13. Implement `wakil query` using QMD results and memory search.
1589	14. Implement source records for ingests.
1590	15. Implement text transcript ingest.
1591	16. Implement article URL ingest.
1592	17. Implement candidate memory extraction.
1593	18. Implement candidate relationship extraction.
1594	19. Implement diff preview for proposed note changes.
1595	20. Implement memory list, promote, reject, and archive commands.
1596	21. Implement git branch creation for ingests.
1597	22. Implement commit convention helpers.
1598	23. Implement initial `wakil dream --recent`.
1599	24. Add tests with a small fixture Markdown knowledge base.
1600	25. Write docs for QMD integration, memory lifecycle, and git workflow.
1601	
1602	---
1603	
1604	## First Milestone
1605	
1606	The first milestone should be:
1607	
1608	> A local CLI tool that initializes a Markdown knowledge-base workspace, indexes notes, searches with QMD, answers grounded questions, ingests text/article sources, proposes memories and note changes, and uses git branches/commits for reviewable modifications.
1609	
1610	This is enough to validate the core idea without building unnecessary platform infrastructure.
1611	
1612	---
1613	
1614	## Design Biases
1615	
1616	Prefer:
1617	
1618	```text id="9hb2du"
1619	simple local workflows
1620	Markdown as source of truth
1621	SQLite as operational store
1622	QMD as first-class search
1623	git-native changes
1624	clear memory lifecycle
1625	human review
1626	rich CLI output
1627	grounded citations
1628	explicit commands
1629	small composable services
1630	```
1631	
1632	Avoid:
1633	
1634	```text id="brzeiq"
1635	remote runtimes
1636	complex permissions
1637	large agent frameworks
1638	hidden background behavior
1639	automatic rewriting without review
1640	multi-agent orchestration
1641	premature graph databases
1642	opaque memory systems
1643	overly abstract plugin architectures
1644	hosted product assumptions
1645	```
1646	
1647	---
1648	
1649	## Examples
1650	
1651	### Example Knowledge Base Structure
1652	
1653	`wakil` should expect a practical, file-native Markdown knowledge base with a mix of durable notes, raw sources, journals, drafts, and operating instructions.
1654	
1655	A representative structure:
1656	
1657	```text
1658	.
1659	├── bin
1660	│    ├── qmd-reindex.sh
1661	│    └── qmd-setup.sh
1662	├── companies
1663	├── concepts
1664	├── drafts
1665	├── journal
1666	│    ├── 2025
1667	│    ├── 2026
1668	│    ├── reflections
1669	│    └── undated
1670	├── media
1671	│    └── articles
1672	├── meetings
1673	│    ├── 2025
1674	│    └── 2026
1675	├── people
1676	├── projects
1677	├── sources
1678	│    ├── articles
1679	│    ├── audio
1680	│    ├── clippings
1681	│    ├── messages
1682	│    ├── screenshots
1683	│    ├── transcripts
1684	│    ├── tweets
1685	│    └── videos
1686	├── AGENTS.md
1687	├── README.md
1688	├── RESOLVER.md
1689	└── SCHEMA.md
1690	```
1691	
1692	### Directory Expectations
1693	
1694	| Path                   | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                               |
1695	| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
1696	| `bin/`                 | Local helper scripts for knowledge-base maintenance, such as QMD setup and reindexing. `wakil` may call these when explicitly requested, but should not assume every workspace has identical scripts. |
1697	| `companies/`           | Durable notes about companies, organizations, vendors, employers, prospects, or institutions.                                                                                                         |
1698	| `concepts/`            | Evergreen concept notes. This is likely one of the most important areas for synthesis, linking, and dream outputs.                                                                                    |
1699	| `drafts/`              | Work-in-progress writing, incomplete notes, rough outlines, and material not yet promoted into durable knowledge.                                                                                     |
1700	| `journal/`             | Chronological personal or work notes. Useful for recency-aware queries, reflection, and identifying how ideas evolved over time.                                                                      |
1701	| `journal/YYYY/`        | Year-specific journal entries.                                                                                                                                                                        |
1702	| `journal/reflections/` | Higher-level reflections that may cut across daily or dated entries.                                                                                                                                  |
1703	| `journal/undated/`     | Journal-like material without a clear date.                                                                                                                                                           |
1704	| `media/articles/`      | Curated or durable article notes, summaries, or responses. This is distinct from raw ingested article sources.                                                                                        |
1705	| `meetings/`            | Meeting notes organized by year. These may contain decisions, follow-ups, participants, and project context.                                                                                          |
1706	| `people/`              | Durable notes about people. Useful for resolving names, relationships, meetings, organizations, and collaboration history.                                                                            |
1707	| `projects/`            | Project notes, plans, decisions, status summaries, and related working material.                                                                                                                      |
1708	| `sources/`             | Raw or lightly processed source material brought into the knowledge base.                                                                                                                             |
1709	| `sources/articles/`    | Raw article captures, extracted article text, or source metadata for articles.                                                                                                                        |
1710	| `sources/audio/`       | Audio files or metadata for recordings that may later be transcribed.                                                                                                                                 |
1711	| `sources/clippings/`   | Small captured excerpts from web pages, documents, chats, or other sources.                                                                                                                           |
1712	| `sources/messages/`    | Exported or pasted message threads.                                                                                                                                                                   |
1713	| `sources/screenshots/` | Screenshots or screenshot metadata.                                                                                                                                                                   |
1714	| `sources/transcripts/` | Meeting, call, video, or audio transcripts.                                                                                                                                                           |
1715	| `sources/tweets/`      | Tweet/X thread captures or metadata.                                                                                                                                                                  |
1716	| `sources/videos/`      | Video links, transcripts, captions, or metadata.                                                                                                                                                      |
1717	
1718	### How `wakil` Should Use This Structure
1719	
1720	`wakil` should not require this exact structure, but it should be able to take advantage of it when present.
1721	
1722	On workspace initialization, `wakil` should:
1723	
1724	1. Detect the presence of `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `SCHEMA.md`, and `RESOLVER.md`.
1725	2. Index their contents as high-priority workspace context.
1726	3. Detect standard directories such as `concepts/`, `people/`, `projects/`, `meetings/`, `journal/`, and `sources/`.
1727	4. Use `SCHEMA.md` to understand metadata conventions before proposing new files.
1728	5. Use `RESOLVER.md` to understand where a file should be stored.
1729	6. Use `AGENTS.md` as operational guidance for agent behavior.
1730	7. Treat `sources/` as raw material and durable note directories such as `concepts/`, `people/`, `projects/`, and `meetings/` as user-facing knowledge artifacts.
1731	
1732	The basic distinction should be:
1733	
1734	```text
1735	sources/     = raw or lightly processed input material
1736	drafts/      = working material
1737	concepts/    = durable evergreen ideas
1738	people/      = durable person/entity notes
1739	companies/   = durable organization notes
1740	projects/    = durable project context
1741	meetings/    = structured meeting knowledge
1742	journal/     = chronological personal/work context
1743	```
1744	
1745	This structure should help `wakil` make better placement, linking, memory, and synthesis decisions without hard-coding the knowledge base too tightly.
1746	
1747	
1748	### Top-Level Markdown Files
1749	
1750	| File          | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
1751	| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
1752	| `README.md`   | Human-facing overview of the knowledge base: what it contains, how it is organized, and how to work with it. `wakil` should read this early when initializing or answering workspace-level questions.                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
1753	| `AGENTS.md`   | Instructions for AI agents operating in this knowledge base. This should define behavioral rules, writing conventions, safety constraints, preferred workflows, and repository-specific guidance. `wakil` should treat this as high-priority operating context.                                                                                                                                                 |
1754	| `SCHEMA.md`   | Shape and formatting rules for knowledge-base pages. This defines entity types, YAML frontmatter standards, filename conventions, page structure, source attribution, confidence markers, wikilink conventions, and templates. `wakil` should consult this before creating or editing any page so generated notes match the vault’s conventions.                                                                |
1755	| `RESOLVER.md` | Routing rules for where knowledge belongs. This is the authority for deciding whether material should become a person, company, meeting, project, concept, idea, organization note, journal entry, source, archive item, inbox item, or sensitive note. `wakil` should consult this before creating or moving pages, especially when deciding between concepts and projects or when handling sensitive content. |
1756	
1757	#### How `wakil` Should Use `SCHEMA.md` and `RESOLVER.md`
1758	
1759	`SCHEMA.md` and `RESOLVER.md` have distinct responsibilities:
1760	
1761	```text id="h51d6h"
1762	RESOLVER.md = where knowledge goes
1763	SCHEMA.md   = how the resulting page is shaped
1764	```
1765	
1766	Before creating, moving, or substantially editing a note, `wakil` should load both files.
1767	
1768	`wakil` should use `RESOLVER.md` to decide the canonical destination, for example:
1769	
1770	```text id="9s3y32"
1771	people/
1772	companies/
1773	meetings/
1774	sources/
1775	projects/
1776	concepts/
1777	journal/
1778	```
1779	
1780	`wakil` should use `SCHEMA.md` to determine the page & metadata format, for example:
1781	
1782	```text id="zidshj"
1783	filename slug
1784	frontmatter fields
1785	name vs title usage
1786	page heading
1787	Compiled Truth section
1788	Timeline / Log section
1789	source attribution
1790	confidence markers
1791	wikilink style
1792	attachment placement
1793	```
1794	
1795	Important behavior:
1796	
1797	1. `wakil` should treat filenames as stable entity identifiers.
1798	2. `wakil` should use lower-case kebab-case filenames.
1799	3. `wakil` should preserve the Compiled Truth / Timeline split on important entity pages.
1800	4. `wakil` should treat the Compiled Truth section as current synthesized state.
1801	5. `wakil` should treat the Timeline / Log section as append-only evidence history.
1802	6. `wakil` should prefer Obsidian-style wikilinks for internal entities.
1803	7. `wakil` should preserve useful existing wikilinks.
1804	8. `wakil` should use root-relative paths rather than relative paths when creating Markdown links.
1805	9. `wakil` should place attachments next to the owning note in a sibling folder with the same slug.
1806	10. `wakil` should warn on sensitive assessments, feedback, compensation, etc.
1807	11. `wakil` should not surface `sensitive/` content in summaries, exports, or shared contexts without explicit instruction.
1808	
1809	### Routing Before Shaping
1810	
1811	The correct note-creation sequence is:
1812	
1813	```text id="tvj5ey"
1814	1. Read RESOLVER.md.
1815	2. Decide where the knowledge belongs.
1816	3. Read SCHEMA.md.
1817	4. Select the right page schema.
1818	5. Create or update the note according to that schema.
1819	6. Use git diff for review before committing.
1820	```
1821	
1822	For example:
1823	
1824	| Input                                  | Resolver Decision            | Schema Decision                                          |
1825	| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
1826	| A new person mentioned in a transcript | `people/first-last.md`       | `type: person`, `name: First Last`, no `title:`          |
1827	| A raw transcript                       | `sources/transcripts/`       | `type: source`, `origin: transcript`                     |
1828	| A synthesized meeting note             | `meetings/<date>-topic.md`   | `type: meeting`, `title:`, `date:`, attendees, decisions |
1829	| A reusable mental model                | `concepts/<slug>.md`         | `type: concept`, `name:`, aliases, domain, maturity      |
1830	| A time-bound work effort               | `projects/<scope>/<slug>.md` | `type: project`, `name:`, status, owner, stakeholders    |
1831	| Performance feedback                   | `sensitive/`                 | `type: assessment`, `sensitive: true`                    |
1832	
1833	### Implication for `wakil`
1834	
1835	`wakil` should not hard-code all routing and schema rules directly into Python.
1836	
1837	Instead, it should:
1838	
1839	1. detect and index `SCHEMA.md` and `RESOLVER.md`;
1840	2. treat them as high-priority workspace instructions;
1841	3. extract a small amount of structured guidance from them where useful;
1842	4. cite them when explaining why it placed or shaped a note a certain way;
1843	5. fail safely by proposing a destination instead of writing when routing is ambiguous.
1844	
1845	The practical rule is:
1846	
1847	```text id="s9v1w3"
1848	When routing is unclear, propose.
1849	When schema is clear, conform.
1850	When content is sensitive, protect.
1851	```
1852	
1853	---
1854	
1855	## Summary
1856	
1857	`wakil` should start as a simple, pragmatic, local-first Python CLI for knowledge work over a Markdown knowledge base.
1858	
1859	The essential foundation is:
1860	
1861	```text id="0cakzv"
1862	Markdown knowledge base
1863	SQLite memory/index
1864	QMD search
1865	git-native workflow
1866	rich CLI
1867	source ingest
1868	query and synthesis
1869	uniform memory model
1870	relationship discovery
1871	dream reports
1872	```
1873	
1874	The long-term direction may include richer graph exploration, GitHub Actions, automated review flows, and deeper synthesis. But the first version should remain focused:
1875	
1876	> Help one local user make better use of a Markdown knowledge base.
1877
